newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa says it's surprised over Zaire talks hitch.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa says it's surprised over Zaire talks hitch.

text.p: South Africa said on Wednesday it was surprised at an apparent hitch to planned peace talks on Zaire's civil war and urged both sides to hurry to the negotiating table.

Doubts have grown over a planned face-to-face meeting on a South African warship between ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila after a U.S. source told Reuters Mobutu had turned down the offer of talks at sea.
South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told state radio he had not expected the setback.
"It is a surprise to us, and we will have to try to determine where it's coming from and what the basis of it is," he said.

"As far as we're cgncerned the urgency of the situation necessitates that the talks start very quickly...we would urge both parties not to hesitate any more, and not to cause any more delays, and to move quickly to the negotiating table."

On Tuesday South Africa said it had secured agreement from both sides in the conflict to meet aboard the naval supply ship Outeniqua in international waters. The Outeniqua is already waiting off the Zairean coast.
But a source travelling with U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson has said Mobutu told Richardson he would not attend the talks, which were to be presided over by President Nelson Mandela.
"Mobutu told Richardson there is no way he would be travelling to a ship for talks with Kabila. So once again the venue for the face-to-face meeting remains a problem," the source said.
South African foreign ministry spokesman Pieter Swanepoel said South Africa was still trying to confirm the reports. "If it is reported accurately it obviously complicates things," he said.

Swanepoel added that U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was on his way to the region to clarify the situation. U.N. sources said Sahnoun was heading first for the Angolan capital Luanda to see President Eduardo dos Santos.
Diplomatic sources said the row over the talks was a fresh blow. "It is delaying matters. We now need another 24 hours to get back to where we were yesterday (Tuesday)," one source said.

Kabila's forces have been battling since October to oust the cancer-stricken Mobutu and have captured more than half the vast central African country. They are now closing in on the capital of Kinshasa -- the only major city they do not hold.
